newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY-MARKGRAAFF QUITS IN RACE-TAPE ROW.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY-MARKGRAAFF QUITS IN RACE-TAPE ROW.

text.p: Andre Markgraaff's troubled reign as manager of South Africa's Springboks ended in tears on Tuesday when he resigned after tacitly admitting making racist comments in a secretly recorded conversation.
"It's a tragic situation but I feel in the interests of the game it is the only way out," he told a hastily called news conference in his diamond-mining home town of Kimberley.

The South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) was to have met on Wednesday to investigate allegations that Markgraaff was the man making racist slurs in Afrikaans in a secretly taped conversation broadcast on national television on Monday.
The man called SARFU's black vice-president Mluleki George a "fucking kaffir", using a highly offensive local insult.

The incident has dealt a fresh damaging blow to the image of South African rugby, which has faced much criticism that -- more than two years into the new democratic era -- it has still not shaken off the country's racist apartheid past.
Markgraaff told the news conference at his home Griqualand West rugby union club that he could not recall making the comments but might have done so.
"I'm not making excuses. If I said it I ask for forgiveness," he said. "I wish to apologise to blacks in this country and also to the whites for embarrassing them."
SARFU chief executive Rian Oberholzer said that they had not been officially told of Markgraaff's resignation. "If indeed he has resigned we may well accept it," he said.
The SARFU chief executive had already called Markgraaff to Wednesday's meeting in Johannesburg to discuss the allegations.
Markgraaff said he learned of the existence of the tape last November, on the eve of the first Springbok test against France.
"I recognised at the time it was to jeopardise the tour and further break me," said Markgraaff, choking back tears.
Markgraaff was flanked by representatives of the Griqualand West rugby union who said the tape was recorded by disgruntled former Griquas player Andre Bester, known for his far-right sympathies.
Markgraaff, detailing steps he had taken to broaden participation in rugby to all races, added: "I'm no racist and my track record speaks for itself."

Markgraaff, who took over after victorious 1995 World Cup coach Kitch Christie resigned last April, had been due to lead South Africa into a three-test series against the British Lions in May and June.

He won eight of his 13 matches in 1996 and looked, by ending the season with six successive victories, to have ridden a storm of protest which blew up after he dropped World Cup winning skipper Francois Pienaar, who now plays in England for London club Saracens.
The Springboks seemed to have buried rugby's past as a "white" game reviled by blacks when they won the 1995 World Cup on home soil.
President Nelson Mandela came on to the pitch in Pienaar's Number 6 green and yellow jersey and embraced the team as "our boys", a sign of reconciliation typical of him.
But things have turned sour again since.

Sports Minister Steve Tshwete last year accused rugby administrators of lacking commitment to bringing blacks into the game and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, less forgiving than Mandela, openly cheered New Zealand's All Blacks instead.
Old wounds were also exacerbated during the All Blacks' visit when white Springbok fans waved the old apartheid-era orange, white and blue South African flag.
